content_voiceover: This pedigree from the same MYH9 case demonstrates classic autosomal dominant inheritance, affected individuals appear in generations one, two, and three, and both males and females are affected, with roughly half of each generation's offspring inheriting the trait. Platelet counts are labeled for several family members, ranging from about seven thousand to thirty-five thousand per microliter, numbers that look alarmingly low, yet these patients are typically asymptomatic or have only mild bruising, because the giant platelets are functionally competent per platelet even though the total count is reduced. A key board pitfall is that automated hematology analyzers often misclassify giant platelets as red cells or misidentify platelet clumps, producing a falsely low or spuriously variable platelet count, so any unexplained thrombocytopenia with a family history and mild bleeding symptoms warrants manual peripheral smear review before starting immunosuppressive therapy for presumed ITP.
keypoints: Autosomal dominant: affected across every generation, both sexes
Platelet counts markedly low (7,000-35,000/uL) yet mild symptoms
Automated analyzers can misclassify giant platelets, falsifying counts
Manual smear review is essential to avoid ITP misdiagnosis
keypoint_voiceover: This family tree shows autosomal dominant transmission of the MYH9 disorder, with affected members in every generation and platelet counts as low as seven thousand per microliter, despite only mild bleeding. Remember that automated counters can miscount giant platelets, so a manual smear is required to catch this before someone is mislabeled with ITP and started on unnecessary steroids.
